method: Rebuild from primary text. Cal. Civ. Code §§1541, 1542 and 3513 were fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and read; Winet v. Price was read in full on CourtListener. The previous record for this clause was a re-check against Winet's opinion text made when no statutory publisher was reachable; §1542 itself had never been opened. Assertions describe the REBUILT body.
queries: Winet Price Civil Code 1542 general release unknown claims waiver

assertions.text: a general release does not extend to claims the releasing party does not know or suspect to exist at the time of execution and that, if known, would have materially affected the settlement
assertions.note: §1542, verbatim as amended by Stats. 2018, Ch. 157 (SB 1431) effective January 1, 2019. The 2019 wording adds 'or releasing party' and 'or released party' to the older 'creditor'/'debtor' formulation. Winet, decided in 1992, quotes the older text — which is exactly the staleness risk the previous clause's own defect list identified.

assertions.text: the benefit of §1542 is one the releasing party may waive
assertions.note: §1542 says nothing about waiver. §3513 supplies the rule: 'Any one may waive the advantage of a law intended solely for their benefit.' §1541 supplies the mechanism by which a release extinguishes an obligation. See gaps — no decision was read that expressly ties §1542's waivability to §3513.

assertions.text: quoting the section is not what makes the waiver effective; what matters is conscious understanding of what is being given up
assertions.note: Winet, restating Casey v. Proctor: the purpose of §1542 'was to prevent the mere recital in the release to that effect from barring a claim for injuries later discovered in the absence of a showing of a conscious understanding'. The previous body stated the drafting convention as a rule of law — quote it in full or the release fails — which §1542 does not impose.

assertions.text: an express waiver negotiated at arm's length with the advice of counsel has been enforced against a party who later said he had not known of the claim
assertions.note: Winet's holding on its facts, quoted below. The clause now describes the circumstances that decided it rather than presenting the outcome as automatic.

priorDefects: contradicted: 'shall expressly waive Civil Code §1542, quoting it in full, or it will not extend to claims the releasing party did not know or suspect to exist'. §1542 imposes no quotation requirement and the consequence is not automatic. The rule the cases state is about conscious understanding.
omitted: that the section was amended effective 1 January 2019, so a form quoting the pre-2019 wording quotes a section that no longer reads that way.
omitted: that the outcome turns on the releasing party's understanding and whether they were advised — the facts Winet actually rested on.
uncited: the waivability of §1542 was asserted with no authority. It rests on Civ. Code §3513.
gaps: No decision was read that expressly grounds §1542's waivability in §3513. The link is this rebuild's reasoning from two statutory texts, and it should be checked by a reviewer rather than taken from here.

Casey v. Proctor (1963) 59 Cal.2d 97 is the source of the conscious-understanding standard and was read only as Winet quotes it. Casey's own reasoning, and how far it is confined to personal-injury settlements with unrepresented claimants, was not examined.
Whether a §1542 waiver reaches claims that had not accrued at the date of the release, as distinct from accrued claims the party did not know about, was not researched.
Winet is a 1992 Court of Appeal decision. Nothing more recent construing the amended §1542 was searched for.

judicialQuotations.case: Winet v. Price (Cal. Ct. App. 1992) 4 Cal.App.4th 1159 — quoting Casey v. Proctor (1963) 59 Cal.2d 97
judicialQuotations.quote: its purpose was to prevent the mere recital in the release to that effect from barring a claim for injuries later discovered in the absence of a showing of a conscious understanding that if injuries were suffered which had not yet manifest...

judicialQuotations.case: Winet v. Price (Cal. Ct. App. 1992) 4 Cal.App.4th 1159
judicialQuotations.quote: With this knowledge and the advice of counsel concerning the language of (and the import of waiving) section 1542, Winet expressly assumed the risk of unknown claims. ... Finally, Winet was represented by his own counsel, who explained to Winet the import of the release in general and of the waiver of section 1542 in particular. Under these circumstances we may not give credence to a claim that a party did not intend clear and direct language to be effective.

currencyCaveat: Winet quotes §1542 in its pre-2019 form ('claims which the creditor does not know or suspect to exist in his favor'). The 2018 amendment added the releasing-party and released-party language. The proposition relied on here — conscious understanding, not a form of words — turns on the purpose of the section rather than its wording, but nobody has confirmed that a post-2019 court has said so. The first quotation above is truncated in the source excerpt at 'had not yet manifest...' and should be re-read in full before it is quoted where a reader will rely on it.
